\chapter{Se Lo --- The Pair That Does Not Exist}
\label{ch:se-for-le}
\hlchaptermodality{99}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can turn le or les into se in front of lo, la, los or las.}

Complete ES-C47-se-lo: produce se lo digo, name the four words that trigger the change, and count the readings se lo digo allows.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[se lo]{se lo — the pair that does not exist}

\label{lesson:ES-C47-se-lo}



\begin{quote}
Person first, then thing. So \textquotedblleft{}I tell it to him\textquotedblright{} should be \emph{le} plus \emph{lo} plus \emph{digo}. Say that out loud: \emph{\textbf{le lo digo}}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: nobody says that}]
Your mouth probably objected before your grammar did. \emph{Le lo} is two nearly identical syllables in a row, and Spanish will not say it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{In front of \emph{lo}, \emph{la}, \emph{los} or \emph{las}, the pronouns \emph{le} and \emph{les} become \emph{se}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textasciitilde{}\textasciitilde{}Le lo digo.\textasciitilde{}\textasciitilde{}} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{Se lo} digo.} — I tell it to him. \emph{\textasciitilde{}\textasciitilde{}Les la hago.\textasciitilde{}\textasciitilde{}} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{Se la} hago.} — I make it for them.
\end{quote}

Everything else about the sentence is unchanged. The order is still person then thing. The slot is still in front of the verb. \textbf{Only the first word's shape changes}, and it changes for one reason: what follows it.

Note what \emph{se} does \textbf{not} tell you. \emph{Le} already refused to mark gender, and \emph{se} goes further — it does not mark number either:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Se lo digo} — to him. To her. To you. To them. To you all.
\end{quote}

Five readings, one word. Context does all the work, and if you need to be precise you add it in words rather than in the pronoun.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le lo digo\textquotedblright{} once, badly, and then \textquotedblleft{}se lo digo\textquotedblright{} — feel why
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Se lo digo\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Se la hago\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}I tell it to him\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Se lo digo}}.) What happened to \emph{le}? (It became \emph{\textbf{se}} in front of \emph{lo}.) Next: \textbf{why} it became \emph{se} — and it is not the reason almost everyone assumes.
\end{tcolorbox}
